headline: GAO Sets a Three-Step Test for Whether Federal Programs Work
dek: The watchdog says agencies need measurable goals, relevant data and routine use of results to judge programs that collectively spend trillions of dollars each year.

sources.title: Federal Programs: Assessing and Improving Effectiveness

lead.creator: APK
lead.rightsBasis: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 license documented on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: The Government Accountability Office headquarters in Washington. GAO says agencies need a repeatable process to determine whether federal programs deliver intended results.
lead.alt: The concrete Government Accountability Office headquarters rises along a Washington street.

charts.caption: GAO's performance-management cycle is to define measurable goals, collect relevant data and use results to improve decisions.
charts.alt: Graphic lists three performance-management steps: define goals, collect data and use results.

charts.caption: GAO distinguishes process, outcome and impact evaluations as different ways to understand whether and why a program works.
charts.alt: Graphic lists process, outcome and impact evaluations.

paragraphs: Federal agencies should use a three-step performance-management cycle to determine whether programs are solving the problems they were created to address, the Government Accountability Office said in a July overview.

The cycle begins with clear, measurable goals, continues with collecting relevant performance data and ends with managers using those results to improve decisions. GAO says the work must be repeated rather than treated as a one-time compliance exercise.

The stakes reach across programs that collectively spend trillions of dollars each year on health care, public safety, disaster support and other services. Without goals and outcome data, Congress and agency leaders cannot reliably judge whether those dollars produce intended results.

GAO distinguishes inputs, such as money available, and outputs, such as the number of people served, from outcomes that describe whether people's lives or public conditions improved in the intended way.

Programs also frequently overlap across agencies. When related programs use different goals or incomplete data, policymakers have less ability to compare their performance, streamline duplicative work or direct resources toward stronger results.

The report points to 15 programs serving pregnant women, young children and their families. Twelve had established performance-management processes; GAO recommended that one program each at Agriculture, Health and Human Services and Veterans Affairs fully develop the missing pieces.

Performance measures can serve as an early-warning system, but GAO says additional evidence is needed to determine effectiveness. Process evaluations test implementation, outcome evaluations examine alignment with desired results and impact evaluations compare results with what would have happened without the program.

In a 2020 survey, about one-third of federal managers reported access to robust program evaluations. That historical survey does not establish the current share, but it illustrates the evidence gap GAO says agencies must close.

The framework is not a finding that every federal program fails. It is a test for whether leaders have enough evidence to identify problems, improve delivery and explain the return on public spending.
facts: GAO describes a three-step performance-management process.
The steps are defining goals, collecting relevant data and using results.
Twelve of 15 reviewed programs for pregnant women and young children had established processes.
GAO recommended improvements at three remaining programs.
About one-third of managers in a 2020 survey reported access to robust evaluations.
uncertainty: The report synthesizes prior GAO work and does not score every federal program.
The 2020 survey result is historical and should not be treated as a current government-wide rate.
seoTitle: GAO's three-step test for federal program effectiveness
seoDescription: GAO says federal programs need measurable goals, relevant data and routine use of results to show whether they work.

headline: NIH Opens ORIVA to Scale Human-Based Research and Reduce Animal Use
dek: The new office will coordinate tissue models, computational tools and other New Approach Methodologies across NIH and with regulators.
entities: Office of Research Innovation, Validation, and Application
Division of Program Coordination, Planning, and Strategic Initiatives
Department of Health and Human Services

sources.title: NIH launches new office to advance human-based research and reduce animal use

lead.creator: Diane A. Reid / National Cancer Institute
lead.rightsBasis: U.S. government public-domain photograph documented by NIH and Wikimedia Commons.
lead.attribution: Diane A. Reid / National Cancer Institute
lead.caption: A National Cancer Institute scientist transfers samples in a laboratory. NIH created ORIVA to coordinate the development and validation of human-based research methods.
lead.alt: A laboratory scientist uses a pipette to transfer samples into a flask.

charts.caption: ORIVA will coordinate New Approach Methodologies including 3D human tissue models and computational tools.
charts.alt: Graphic lists 3D human tissue models, computational tools and other animal-free methods.

charts.caption: One ORIVA division will support research innovation; the other will coordinate evaluation and acceptance across agencies.
charts.alt: Graphic shows ORIVA's research-support and evaluation-coordination divisions.

paragraphs: The National Institutes of Health has created an office charged with accelerating human-based research technologies and reducing or replacing animal use where appropriate.

The Office of Research Innovation, Validation, and Application, known as ORIVA, will coordinate NIH-wide work on New Approach Methodologies. NIH listed 3D human tissue models, computational tools and other animal-free methods among the technologies in scope.

ORIVA is housed in the Division of Program Coordination, Planning, and Strategic Initiatives within the NIH Office of the Director. That placement gives it an agency-wide coordination role rather than tying it to one disease institute.

NIH said the office will have two divisions. One will support innovation through funding opportunities, research infrastructure and training; the other will coordinate a multi-agency effort to evaluate and accept new methods.

Validation and regulatory translation are central to the plan. A laboratory method can be scientifically promising without yet being standardized, reproducible or accepted for a particular regulatory decision.

NIH said differences between animal and human biology can limit how well findings translate. Human-based methods may add tools that are more replicable, efficient or directly relevant to human disease, while traditional animal models have also contributed to scientific knowledge and treatments.
The announcement does not impose a blanket end to animal research. It says NIH will assess where animal use can be reduced or eliminated and scale alternatives when evidence supports doing so.

The office's effectiveness will therefore depend on more than the number of methods funded. Researchers and regulators will need transparent standards for validation, evidence about where a method performs well and clarity about situations in which it does not.

ORIVA establishes a central institutional route for that work: fund human-focused technologies, build the infrastructure to test them and coordinate their acceptance across the research and regulatory systems.
facts: NIH announced ORIVA on June 15, 2026.
ORIVA will coordinate NIH-wide New Approach Methodologies.
The office is housed in DPCPSI in the NIH Office of the Director.
One division will support innovation and one will coordinate evaluation and acceptance.
NIH explicitly included 3D human tissue models and computational tools.
uncertainty: The announcement does not quantify how quickly validated methods will replace specific animal models.
Performance and regulatory acceptance will vary by method and intended use.
seoTitle: NIH launches ORIVA for human-based research methods
seoDescription: NIH's new ORIVA office will develop, validate and scale human-based research methods while reducing animal use where appropriate.

headline: Smithsonian STEM Gift Targets 40 Communities and 24 Schools
dek: A $2.3 million Caterpillar Foundation donation will fund teacher training, hands-on resources and an AI learning guide across 21 states over three years.

sources.title: Caterpillar Foundation To Give $2.3 Million to Smithsonian in Celebration of America's 250th Anniversary

lead.creator: P. Hughes
lead.rightsBasis: Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 license documented on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.attribution: P. Hughes / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
lead.caption: The Smithsonian Institution Building seen from the Haupt Garden. A new gift will extend Smithsonian science-education resources into communities across 21 states.
lead.alt: The red sandstone Smithsonian Castle rises beyond a green garden in Washington.

charts.caption: The three-year Smithsonian effort is designed to reach 40 communities in 21 states.
charts.alt: Graphic shows 40 communities, 21 states and a three-year program.

charts.caption: Twenty-four schools will receive sponsored participation in the STEAM Schools of Distinction program.
charts.alt: Graphic shows 24 sponsored schools plus professional learning and virtual support.

paragraphs: The Smithsonian will use a $2.3 million Caterpillar Foundation donation to provide science, technology, engineering and mathematics programming in 40 communities across 21 states over the next three years.
The Smithsonian Science Education Center will provide professional development for educators, hands-on teaching resources and virtual training, according to the institution's July announcement.

Twenty-four middle and high schools will receive sponsored participation in the Smithsonian STEAM Schools of Distinction program, which supports schools integrating science, technology, engineering, arts and mathematics across teaching and learning.
For those schools, the Smithsonian said it will provide immersive professional learning, ongoing virtual support and access to museums and research centers.

The gift also funds an AI-focused learning guide. Planned lessons will ask students to identify uses of artificial intelligence in their communities, investigate tools used in the STEM workforce and practice applying AI to local needs.

About 40 communities will receive virtual teacher-training sessions intended to connect classrooms with relevant Smithsonian resources. The release does not yet identify every participating school or community.
The institution described the gift as part of the Smithsonian Campaign for Our Shared Future and tied it to the United States' 250th-anniversary year.

Donation size and geographic reach do not by themselves measure learning gains. Useful evaluation would track which educators participate, how resources are used and whether schools sustain the work after the three-year period.
The immediate commitment is concrete: 24 sponsored schools, training across roughly 40 communities and a national set of classroom resources built around STEM and responsible exploration of AI.
facts: The Caterpillar Foundation donation is $2.3 million.
The program is intended for 40 communities in 21 states.
The planned term is three years.
Twenty-four schools will receive sponsored participation.
The Smithsonian will develop an AI-focused learning guide.
uncertainty: The release does not name all participating schools or communities.
Program reach does not establish eventual student-learning outcomes.
seoTitle: Smithsonian $2.3 million STEM gift reaches 40 communities
seoDescription: A Caterpillar Foundation gift will fund Smithsonian STEM resources, teacher training and 24 STEAM Schools of Distinction.

headline: IMF Sees Ireland's Domestic Growth Slowing to 2.5% as Inflation Rises
dek: The 2026 Article IV review says Ireland remains resilient but faces concentrated corporate-tax exposure, energy risks and persistent housing constraints.

sources.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2026 Article IV Consultation with Ireland
Ireland: 2026 Article IV Consultation—Press Release and Staff Report

lead.creator: Creevylea
lead.rightsBasis: Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 license documented on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: The Custom House beside the River Liffey in Dublin. The IMF says Ireland enters a more uncertain period from a position of economic strength.
lead.alt: Dublin's domed Custom House stands beside the River Liffey under a blue sky.

charts.caption: The IMF projects modified domestic demand growth to moderate from almost 5% in 2025 to about 2.5% in 2026–27.
charts.alt: Graphic shows Ireland modified domestic demand slowing from almost 5 percent to about 2.5 percent.

charts.caption: Headline inflation is projected at about 3.5% in 2026 before returning to 2% around 2028.
charts.alt: Graphic shows inflation around 3.5 percent in 2026 and 2 percent around 2028.

paragraphs: Ireland's domestic economy is expected to slow while remaining resilient, with modified domestic demand growth easing from almost 5% in 2025 to about 2.5% in 2026 and 2027, the International Monetary Fund said.

Modified domestic demand is closely watched in Ireland because headline gross domestic product can be heavily affected by multinational-company activity. The IMF said consumption and investment supported strong 2025 growth.
Headline inflation stayed near 2% in 2025 but has accelerated with higher energy prices. The fund projects inflation at about 3.5% in 2026 before returning to 2% around 2028.

Ireland's government balance remained in a sizable surplus in 2025, supported by strong corporate income-tax receipts from multinational enterprises. The same concentration is a vulnerability if company profits, tax rules or investment patterns shift.

The fund said export growth is expected to slow significantly in 2026 and the current-account surplus should moderate over the medium term. It assessed risks to growth as tilted down and risks to inflation as tilted up.

Policy recommendations include broadening the tax base, controlling current-spending growth, improving budget credibility and using public investment efficiently rather than assuming unusually strong corporate-tax receipts will persist.
The IMF also urged Ireland to boost housing supply, improve energy security, prepare workers for the AI transition and continue integrating with the European Union energy market.

The projection is conditional on assumptions about energy prices and the global economy. A longer geopolitical shock, sharper trade fragmentation or changes affecting multinational firms could produce materially different outcomes.

The central message is a window rather than a guarantee: Ireland's current fiscal and economic strength creates room to address housing, energy and productivity constraints before external risks become harder to absorb.
facts: Modified domestic demand growth is projected at about 2.5% in 2026–27.
The comparable 2025 growth rate was almost 5%.
Headline inflation is projected at about 3.5% in 2026.
Inflation is projected to return to 2% around 2028.
The IMF identifies reliance on multinational corporate-tax receipts as a vulnerability.
uncertainty: The outlook depends on energy-price, trade and geopolitical assumptions.
Irish GDP and domestic-activity measures can diverge because of multinational-company activity.
seoTitle: IMF projects 2.5% Irish domestic growth and 3.5% inflation
seoDescription: The IMF says Ireland remains resilient but projects slower domestic demand growth and higher 2026 inflation amid external risks.

headline: U.S. Rental Vacancy Rate Holds at 7.3% in Second Quarter
dek: Census estimates put the homeowner vacancy rate at 1.2% and the national homeownership rate at 65.0%, with no statistically significant annual change.

sources.title: Quarterly Residential Vacancies and Homeownership, Second Quarter 2026

lead.creator: Monumenteer2014camper
lead.rightsBasis: Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 license documented on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: Homes in Raleigh's Cameron Village Historic District. Census estimates show national rental and homeowner vacancy rates changed little in the second quarter.
lead.alt: Detached houses line a leafy residential street in Raleigh, North Carolina.

charts.caption: Second-quarter estimates were 7.3% for rental vacancies and 1.2% for homeowner vacancies.
charts.alt: Graphic shows a 7.3 percent rental vacancy rate and 1.2 percent homeowner vacancy rate.

charts.caption: The national homeownership rate was 65.0%, virtually the same as the second quarter of 2025.
charts.alt: Graphic shows a 65.0 percent homeownership rate in both second-quarter 2025 and 2026.

paragraphs: The national rental vacancy rate was 7.3% in the second quarter of 2026, virtually unchanged from the first quarter and not statistically different from a year earlier, the Census Bureau reported.

The second-quarter 2025 rental vacancy estimate was 7.0%, while the first-quarter 2026 estimate was 7.3%. Sampling uncertainty means the apparent annual difference should not be treated as a confirmed change.
The homeowner vacancy rate was 1.2%, compared with 1.1% in both the second quarter of 2025 and the first quarter of 2026. Census said neither comparison was statistically different.
The homeownership rate was 65.0%, virtually the same as the 65.0% estimate a year earlier and not statistically different from the 65.3% first-quarter estimate.
Rental vacancy measures the share of rental inventory that is vacant and available for rent. Homeowner vacancy measures vacant units available for sale as a share of homeowner inventory.

National stability can coexist with substantial differences among regions, metro areas and property types. Local rents, construction, household formation and financing conditions do not move uniformly.

The estimates come from the Current Population Survey and Housing Vacancy Survey and are subject to sampling and nonsampling error. Census explicitly evaluates whether quarter-to-quarter and year-to-year differences are statistically meaningful.

Vacancy rates also do not directly measure affordability. A market can have available units that many households cannot afford, while a low vacancy rate can indicate tight supply without identifying the cause.

The second-quarter release therefore describes a national market with little confirmed movement in its broad tenure indicators: rental vacancy at 7.3%, homeowner vacancy at 1.2% and homeownership at 65.0%.
facts: The second-quarter rental vacancy rate was 7.3%.
The homeowner vacancy rate was 1.2%.
The homeownership rate was 65.0%.
The rental vacancy estimate was virtually the same as first quarter 2026.
Census found no statistically significant annual change in the three headline measures.
uncertainty: Survey estimates are subject to sampling and nonsampling error.
National vacancy and homeownership rates do not measure local affordability or every regional market.
seoTitle: U.S. rental vacancy rate stayed at 7.3% in Q2 2026
seoDescription: Census estimates show 7.3% rental vacancy, 1.2% homeowner vacancy and 65.0% homeownership in the second quarter.

headline: Division I Teams Can Now Add Commercial Patches to Uniforms
dek: An NCAA rule effective August 1 permits two added logos on uniforms and apparel, one on equipment and another for conference championships outside NCAA postseason play.

sources.title: DI Cabinet approves commercial patches for uniforms, equipment and apparel

lead.creator: Jared Winkler
lead.rightsBasis: Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 license documented on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.attribution: Jared Winkler / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
lead.caption: Magness Arena at the University of Denver. Division I programs may now sell additional commercial logo space for regular-season competition.
lead.alt: A snow-covered college sports arena and campus tower stand beneath an overcast winter sky.

charts.caption: Division I teams may add two commercial logos to uniforms and apparel and one to equipment outside NCAA championships.
charts.alt: Graphic shows limits of two added uniform logos and one equipment logo.

charts.caption: Each added logo is limited to 4 square inches, with one additional uniform or apparel logo allowed for conference championships.
charts.alt: Graphic shows a four-square-inch limit and one additional conference-championship logo.

paragraphs: NCAA Division I programs can now place additional commercial logos on uniforms, apparel and equipment under a rule that took effect August 1.
The policy permits up to two added commercial logos on uniforms and apparel and one added logo on equipment during preseason and regular-season competition.
Teams may add one more commercial logo on uniforms and apparel for conference championships. The authorization does not extend to NCAA championship competition.

Each commercial logo is limited to 4 square inches. Playing-rules groups, oversight committees and sport committees are responsible for placement restrictions where logos could interfere with numbers, markings or officiating.
The Division I Cabinet approved the policy in January as schools sought additional revenue sources while expanding direct financial benefits for athletes.
Permission does not require every school or conference to sell every available placement. Institutions can set their own commercial standards within NCAA rules and existing contracts.

The change also separates conference-controlled postseason events from NCAA championships: an added conference-championship patch may be permissible even though NCAA postseason uniforms remain under the tighter national rule.

Actual revenue will depend on audience size, sport, school brand, sponsor demand, conference policy and conflicts with apparel agreements. The NCAA announcement did not publish a forecast of total patch revenue.

The effective rule creates new inventory on Division I uniforms while preserving a different commercial boundary for NCAA championships, adding another visible layer to college sports' changing business model.
facts: The rule took effect August 1, 2026.
Two added commercial logos are allowed on uniforms and apparel.
One added commercial logo is allowed on equipment.
One additional logo is permitted for conference championships.
Each logo is limited to 4 square inches and the policy excludes NCAA championship competition.
uncertainty: The NCAA did not forecast aggregate revenue from the new inventory.
Schools, conferences and existing contracts may impose narrower commercial limits.
seoTitle: NCAA Division I commercial uniform patches are now allowed
seoDescription: A rule effective August 1 lets Division I teams add commercial patches to uniforms, apparel and equipment outside NCAA championships.
